In December 2004, Drew signed a five-year, $55 million contract with the [Los Angeles Dodgers](/wiki/Los_Angeles_Dodgers "Los Angeles Dodgers"),[[12]](#cite_note-12) which included an escape clause after the second year. Roughly halfway through the 2005 season, Drew's season was again cut short after being hit on the wrist by a pitch from [Arizona Diamondbacks](/wiki/Arizona_Diamondbacks "Arizona Diamondbacks")' pitcher [Brad Halsey](/wiki/Brad_Halsey "Brad Halsey").

On September 18, 2006, Drew was part of only the (then) fourth-ever set of back-to-back-to-back-to-back home runs with fellow Dodgers [Jeff Kent](/wiki/Jeff_Kent "Jeff Kent"), [Russell Martin](/wiki/Russell_Martin_(baseball) "Russell Martin (baseball)"), and [Marlon Anderson](/wiki/Marlon_Anderson "Marlon Anderson").[[13]](#cite_note-13)

In 2006, Drew exercised his contract opt-out clause, forgoing $33 million over the next three years to become a [free agent](/wiki/Free_agent "Free agent"). Dodgers general manager [Ned Colletti](/wiki/Ned_Colletti "Ned Colletti") said in a teleconference that he was "surprised how it came down. Everything we had heard, everything that had been written led us to believe the player loved being here."[[14]](#cite_note-14)[[15]](#cite_note-15) This was especially a surprise because a few days before, Drew had told an *[LA Times](/wiki/LA_Times "LA Times")* columnist on how happy he was in LA and that he was looking forward to the upcoming 2007 season. Drew had a very good season, batting .284 with 20 home runs and 100 RBI.

The *Dayton Daily News* reported the October 5, 1905, flight on page 9, with agriculture and business news.[[108]](#cite_note-112)

A few newspapers published articles about the long flights, but no reporters or photographers had been there. The lack of splashy eyewitness press coverage was a major reason for disbelief in Washington, D.C., and Europe, and in journals like *Scientific American*, whose editors doubted the "alleged experiments" and asked how U.S. newspapers, "alert as they are, allowed these sensational performances to escape their notice."[[109]](#cite_note-113)

In October 1904, the brothers were visited by the first of many important Europeans they would befriend in coming years, [Colonel J. E. Capper](/wiki/John_Capper "John Capper"), later superintendent of the [Royal Balloon Factory](/wiki/Royal_Aircraft_Establishment "Royal Aircraft Establishment"). Capper and his wife were visiting the United States to investigate the aeronautical exhibits at the [St. Louis World Fair](/wiki/Louisiana_Purchase_Exposition "Louisiana Purchase Exposition"), but had been given a letter of introduction to both Chanute and the Wrights by [Patrick Alexander](/wiki/Patrick_Young_Alexander "Patrick Young Alexander"). Capper was very favorably impressed by the Wrights, who showed him photographs of their aircraft in flight.[[110]](#cite_note-114)

The Wright brothers were certainly complicit in the lack of attention they received. Fearful of competitors stealing their ideas, and still without a patent, they flew on only one more day after October 5. The **Great Wall of China** ([traditional Chinese](/wiki/Traditional_Chinese_characters "Traditional Chinese characters"): 萬里長城; [simplified Chinese](/wiki/Simplified_Chinese_characters "Simplified Chinese characters"): 万里长城; [pinyin](/wiki/Pinyin "Pinyin"): *Wànlǐ Chángchéng*, literally "ten thousand [*li*](/wiki/Li_(unit) "Li (unit)") long wall") is a series of [fortifications](/wiki/Fortifications "Fortifications") in China. They were built across the historical northern borders of [ancient Chinese states](/wiki/Ancient_Chinese_states "Ancient Chinese states") and [Imperial China](/wiki/Imperial_China "Imperial China") as protection against [various nomadic groups](/wiki/Eurasian_nomads "Eurasian nomads") from the [Eurasian Steppe](/wiki/Eurasian_Steppe "Eurasian Steppe"). The first walls date to the 7th century BC; these were joined together in the [Qin dynasty](/wiki/Qin_dynasty "Qin dynasty").[[4]](#cite_note-nyt-4)[[5]](#cite_note-Brit-5) Successive dynasties expanded the wall system; the best-known sections were built by the [Ming dynasty](/wiki/Ming_dynasty "Ming dynasty") (1368–1644).

To aid in defense, the Great Wall utilized [watchtowers](/wiki/Watchtower "Watchtower"), troop barracks, garrison stations, signaling capabilities through the means of smoke or fire, and its status as a transportation corridor. Other purposes of the Great Wall have included [border controls](/wiki/Border_control "Border control") (allowing control of immigration and emigration, and the imposition of duties on goods transported along the [Silk Road](/wiki/Silk_Road "Silk Road")), and the regulation of trade.[[6]](#cite_note-6)
